title: Miniature giants: investigating limb long bone structure in dwarf proboscideans
summary: Terrestrial vertebrates rely on their skeleton to provide structural support and allow the movement of the body. Heavy, graviportal taxa, such as extant elephants, exhibit numerous adaptive features in their bone anatomy enabling them to withstand their immense weight. Conversely, dwarfing events impose novel biomechanical constraints on the skeleton. The case of dwarf elephants raises the question of how graviportal animals adapt when undergoing drastic size reduction, and whether they retain graviportal features or exhibit paedomorphic traits. In this study, we examine the morphology and microanatomy of the six long bones in two fossil species of dwarf elephants, Palaeoloxodon tiliensis (adults) and P.___falconeri (juveniles), using both quantitative and qualitative approaches (3D geometric morphometrics, virtual slice comparisons, compact bone thickness cartographies). Our results show that in P.___tiliensis , the reduction in body mass is reflected in the morphology and microanatomy of the bones, suggesting a more flexed limb posture and a reduced parasagittal orientation compared to in fully graviportal proboscideans. Despite this shift, several key graviportal adaptations are retained in P.___tiliensis . Additionally, comparisons with early, non-graviportal proboscideans indicate that dwarf elephants exhibit a partial reversion to ancestral limb traits, while maintaining essential weight-bearing features. Finally, adult P.___tiliensis and juvenile P.___falconeri specimens exhibit a medullary area filled with trabecular bone, similar to that of extant elephants. Dwarf elephants are thus not scaled-down versions of their mainland ancestors, but instead display a combination of juvenile, graviportal and ancestral traits reflecting the impact of dwarfism on their evolutionary trajectory.

AI.tldr: This study examines the morphology and microanatomy of long bones in two fossil dwarf elephant species (Palaeoloxodon tiliensis and P. falconeri) and finds that dwarf elephants are not scaled-down versions of their mainland ancestors, but rather display a unique combination of juvenile, graviportal, and ancestral traits reflecting the impact of dwarfism on their evolutionary trajectory.
AI.motivation: To understand how graviportal (heavy, weight-bearing) animals like elephants adapt their skeleton when undergoing drastic size reduction through dwarfism, and whether they retain graviportal features or exhibit paedomorphic (juvenile) traits.
AI.method: Examination of the morphology and microanatomy of all six long bones in two fossil dwarf elephant species (adult P. tiliensis and juvenile P. falconeri) using quantitative and qualitative approaches including 3D geometric morphometrics, virtual slice comparisons, and compact bone thickness cartographies.
AI.result: P. tiliensis shows reduced body mass reflected in bone morphology and microanatomy, with more flexed limb posture and reduced parasagittal orientation compared to fully graviportal proboscideans. However, key graviportal adaptations are retained. Dwarf elephants show partial reversion to ancestral limb traits while maintaining essential weight-bearing features. Both species exhibit medullary areas filled with trabecular bone, similar to extant elephants.
AI.conclusion: Dwarf elephants are not simply scaled-down versions of their mainland ancestors. Instead, they exhibit a combination of juvenile, graviportal, and ancestral traits, reflecting the complex impact of dwarfism on their evolutionary trajectory.

title: The Connectome and the Quest for the Functional Logic of the Drosophila Early Olfactory System
summary: In recent decades, the early olfactory system (EOS) of the fruit fly has become a leading model for studying olfactory processing and associative memory, owing in part to a well-characterized feedforward pathway that feeds the processes underlying associative memory and by examining the role played by a handful of neurons and synapses. The recent completion of dense electron-microscopy connectomes provides high quality visualizations of every cell type, neuron, and synapse along the early olfactory pathway. Yet a wiring diagram, however complete, does not by itself reveal the functional logic of a neural circuit. Reviewing the EOS connectome and synaptome datasets of the past fifteen years, we note that the feedforward pathway is embedded in dense local feedback circuits of large scale multi-input multi-output neurons. A systematic understanding of feedback loop abstractions, and their capacity to govern the input/output transformations at each neuropil stage, is the underlying foundation of the functional logic of the early olfactory circuits. In addition, we argue that a quantitative account of the functional logic requires an explicit model of the odorants present in the natural environment. Consisting of odorant objects, such a model defines the semantics and syntax of olfactory information processing, and calls for new distance measures for classifying the odorant semantics in support of associative memory operations. Furthermore, odor information processing must abide by causality, treating the circuit as a real-time, stage-by-stage cascade of giant local feedback loops.

AI.tldr: This review paper argues that while dense EM connectomes of the fruit fly early olfactory system (EOS) provide complete wiring diagrams, understanding the functional logic of olfactory circuits requires analyzing the dense local feedback loops (multi-input multi-output neurons) embedded within the feedforward pathway, along with an explicit model of natural odorants and a causality-respecting, real-time perspective of stage-by-stage processing.
AI.motivation: The complete connectome of the fruit fly EOS has been mapped, providing every neuron, cell type, and synapse. However, a static wiring diagram alone cannot reveal the functional logic of a neural circuit. The field needs conceptual frameworks that go beyond connectivity to understand how the EOS actually computes and supports associative memory.
AI.method: The paper reviews fifteen years of EOS connectome and synaptome datasets, identifying that the well-characterized feedforward pathway is embedded in dense local feedback circuits of large-scale multi-input multi-output neurons. The authors propose a systematic framework centered on feedback loop abstractions and their role in input/output transformations at each neuropil stage.
AI.result: The review reveals that the feedforward pathway is not a simple linear sequence but is embedded within dense local feedback circuits. It further argues that understanding functional logic requires (1) systematic feedback loop abstractions governing input/output transformations, (2) an explicit model of odorant objects defining the semantics/syntax of olfactory information, and (3) new distance measures for classifying odorant semantics to support associative memory.
AI.conclusion: A quantitative account of the EOS functional logic requires modeling the circuit as a real-time, stage-by-stage cascade of giant local feedback loops, embedded within a properly defined natural odorant environment, respecting causality throughout.

title: Reducing Boolean Networks via Analysis of Dynamic Network Subgraph Behavior
comment: 33 pages, 6 figures, Check this Github repository for codes and more detials: https://github.com/jafarilab/BORNA
summary: Boolean networks provide a compact framework for modeling regulatory systems, yet their rapidly expanding state spaces make systematic dynamical analysis challenging. Here, we systematically enumerate all non-isomorphic two-node signed regulatory subgraphs with their admissible Boolean update rules and exhaustively characterize their state-transition graphs (STGs) under both synchronous and asynchronous updating. By extracting quantitative dynamical descriptors, we move beyond static wiring diagrams toward a behavior-based classification of network structures. The synchronous analysis identifies deterministic fixed-point and cyclic attractor regimes, while the asynchronous analysis captures one-node-at-a-time dynamics through terminal strongly connected components of the asynchronous STGs. Comparing the two update schemes distinguishes dynamical behaviors that are robust across update assumptions from those that depend on synchronous updating. Despite the diversity of graph-rule combinations, many realizations converge to a limited repertoire of dynamical classes, revealing substantial redundancy between structural and dynamical representations. We further propose a testable framework for investigating whether such local dynamical classes can be used to characterize selected subnetworks within larger Boolean models. To facilitate exploration and reproducibility, we developed BORNA, an interactive web application for exploring the complete network catalogue, STGs, and synchronous and asynchronous simulations, available at https://jafarilab.github.io/BORNA/. Together, these results provide a systematic reference for minimal Boolean network dynamics and a foundation for extending behavior-based analysis to larger regulatory systems.

AI.tldr: This paper exhaustively enumerates all non-isomorphic two-node signed Boolean regulatory subgraphs with their admissible update rules, and characterizes their state-transition graphs under both synchronous and asynchronous updating. The analysis reveals that despite structural diversity, many graph-rule combinations converge to a limited number of dynamical classes, highlighting redundancy between structure and dynamics. A web application (BORNA) is provided for exploration and reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Boolean networks are compact models for regulatory systems, but their rapidly expanding state spaces make systematic dynamical analysis challenging. The authors aim to move beyond static wiring diagrams toward a behavior-based classification of minimal network structures, and to compare how different update schemes (synchronous vs. asynchronous) affect dynamical outcomes.
AI.method: The authors systematically enumerate all non-isomorphic two-node signed regulatory subgraphs with admissible Boolean update rules, then exhaustively characterize their state-transition graphs (STGs) under both synchronous and asynchronous updating. They extract quantitative dynamical descriptors for behavior-based classification, comparing deterministic fixed-point/cyclic attractor regimes (synchronous) against terminal strongly connected components of asynchronous STGs. They also develop BORNA, an interactive web application for exploring the catalogue and simulations.
AI.result: Despite diverse graph-rule combinations, many realizations converge to a limited repertoire of dynamical classes, revealing substantial redundancy between structural and dynamical representations. The comparison of update schemes distinguishes behaviors robust across update assumptions from those dependent on synchronous updating. A testable framework is proposed for using local dynamical classes to characterize subnetworks within larger Boolean models.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a systematic reference for minimal Boolean network dynamics and serve as a foundation for extending behavior-based analysis to larger regulatory systems. The BORNA web application facilitates exploration and reproducibility of the complete network catalogue, STGs, and simulations.

authors: Isabel M. V. Guedes de Carvalho
title: Hepatitis C Virus Genotyping with a Transformer Neural Network
summary: This study aims to explore the applicability of Transformer-based models for genetic sequence classification by evaluating their performance in predicting hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotypes and subtypes after fine-tuning. A total of 2,881 HCV whole-genome sequences obtained from the Los Alamos HCV Sequence Database were used, including genotypes 1 to 6 and all confirmed subtypes. Genotypes 7 and 8 were excluded due to an insufficient number of samples. The fine-tuning process was based on several datasets that differed in fragmentation method, data volume per file, and labeling. In genotype classification, fine-tuning strategies employing homogeneous fragmentation and balanced sample distribution resulted in higher performance, with precision ranging from 98.48% to 100%. In contrast, fine-tuning conducted using a fragmentation strategy that caused data imbalance, along with an arbitrary distribution of samples across training files, achieved a precision of 48.12%, which is considered low compared with other models. This configuration, which was also manually evaluated, resulted in a high error rate in genotype 5 prediction due to its low frequency in the datasets used. In subtype classification, the best-performing fine-tuning approach achieved 99.89% accuracy and 99.87% precision. Models that included additional genotypes showed a slight decrease in performance due to the increased complexity of the task. This study demonstrates that, when fine-tuning datasets contain properly fragmented, distributed, and labeled genetic sequences, Transformer-based neural networks can achieve high performance and are a promising approach for HCV genotype and subtype classification.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates Transformer-based models for HCV genotype and subtype classification using 2,881 whole-genome sequences. Fine-tuning strategies with homogeneous fragmentation and balanced sample distribution achieved precision of 98.48-100% for genotype classification, while imbalanced data strategies yielded only 48.12% precision. The best subtype classification approach achieved 99.89% accuracy and 99.87% precision, demonstrating that properly prepared fine-tuning datasets enable Transformer models to perform excellently in viral sequence classification.
AI.motivation: To explore whether Transformer-based models can be effectively applied to genetic sequence classification, specifically for hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype and subtype prediction after fine-tuning, and to understand how dataset preparation strategies affect model performance.
AI.method: Used 2,881 HCV whole-genome sequences from the Los Alamos HCV Sequence Database, covering genotypes 1-6. Fine-tuned Transformer models across multiple datasets that varied in fragmentation method, data volume per file, and labeling strategy. Evaluated both genotype and subtype classification performance.
AI.result: Genotype classification with homogeneous fragmentation and balanced sample distribution achieved 98.48-100% precision. Imbalanced data fragmentation yielded only 48.12% precision with poor genotype 5 prediction. Best subtype classification achieved 99.89% accuracy and 99.87% precision. Models with additional genotypes showed slightly lower performance due to increased task complexity.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based neural networks are a promising approach for HCV genotype and subtype classification when fine-tuning datasets are properly fragmented, distributed, and labeled, enabling high performance comparable to or exceeding other methods.

title: A stochastic dose-response framework for environmentally persistent pathogens
summary: Infectious diseases caused by environmentally persistent pathogens can strongly affect host populations as transmission occurs not only through direct host-host contact but also via indirect exposure to contaminated environments. While in some systems environmental reservoirs help sustain exposure even when infected host numbers are low, reliance on environmental transmission pathway may also increase pathogen extinction risk. Infection risk may depend on both pathogen dose and timing of exposure. Thus, understanding how dose-response, stochasticity, and seasonal changes in host susceptibility or contact rates shape pathogen invasion and persistence remains an important challenge for environmentally transmitted disease systems. To address this, we develop a stochastic dose-response framework that integrates host infection dynamics with an explicit environmental pathogen reservoir. Transmission occurs through both direct contact with infectious hosts and indirect environmental exposure, with infection probability governed by dose-response functions. We focus on stochastic continuous-time Markov chain formulation and use branching process approximation to estimate disease extinction probabilities when infected hosts or environmental pathogen loads are low. We extend the framework to include seasonality in host susceptibility, environmental contact, and host-host contact. As a case study, we apply the model to snake fungal disease. Numerical simulations show that dose-response influences epidemic takeoff and infection levels, while seasonality creates windows of high and low extinction risk. These extinction risks depend strongly on the route and timing of introduction within the seasonal cycle. These results, coupled with global sensitivity analysis, illustrate how stochasticity, nonlinear dose-response, and seasonal timing shape outbreak dynamics for environmentally persistent pathogens.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a stochastic dose-response framework integrating host infection dynamics with an explicit environmental pathogen reservoir to study invasion and persistence of environmentally transmitted pathogens. Using a continuous-time Markov chain with branching process approximation, the model incorporates direct and indirect transmission with dose-response functions, and extends to seasonal effects. Applied to snake fungal disease, simulations reveal that dose-response shapes epidemic takeoff, while seasonality creates windows of variable extinction risk depending on introduction route and timing.
AI.motivation: Environmentally transmitted pathogens are understudied because transmission occurs via both direct host contact and indirect environmental exposure, and infection risk depends on dose and timing. Understanding how dose-response, stochasticity, and seasonality shape pathogen invasion and persistence is a key challenge for these disease systems.
AI.method: A stochastic dose-response framework integrates host infection dynamics with an explicit environmental reservoir. Transmission occurs via direct host-host contact and indirect environmental exposure, with infection probability governed by dose-response functions. A stochastic continuous-time Markov chain formulation with branching process approximation estimates extinction probabilities at low host or pathogen load, extended to include seasonality in host susceptibility, environmental contact, and host-host contact.
AI.result: Numerical simulations on snake fungal disease show dose-response influences epidemic takeoff and infection levels. Seasonality creates windows of high and low extinction risk, with extinction probabilities strongly dependent on the route and timing of introduction within the seasonal cycle. Global sensitivity analysis highlights how stochasticity, nonlinear dose-response, and seasonal timing shape outbreak dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that stochasticity, nonlinear dose-response, and seasonal timing collectively shape outbreak dynamics for environmentally persistent pathogens, providing insights into extinction risk windows and factors governing pathogen invasion and persistence.

title: Correlations at criticality in ecological communities
summary: Ecological communities are continually reshaped by invasion, exclusion, and diversification, processes that naturally drive them toward the boundary of dynamical stability. Near such a boundary, a soft mode relaxes increasingly slowly and, under stochastic forcing, is expected to dominate the fluctuations, effectively reducing the dynamics to one dimension and generating strong positive and negative abundance correlations. Such correlations have therefore been proposed as signatures of an imminent transition. Here we show that this expectation can fail even arbitrarily close to criticality. The reason is that spectral softness does not guarantee stochastic visibility: the soft mode must receive enough environmental forcing to dominate the fluctuation background generated by the remaining modes. We demonstrate this mechanism in three ecological scenarios: a synthetic feasible community, a local community assembled by immigration from a regional pool, and a community generated by repeated diversification. In all three, communities approach marginal stability without developing the near-perfect pairwise correlations predicted by the single-mode picture. Thus, proximity to ecological criticality need not be visible in equal-time pairwise correlations.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that ecological communities approaching marginal (critical) stability may not exhibit the strong pairwise abundance correlations previously proposed as signatures of imminent transitions. The reason is that the soft (slow) mode near criticality may not receive enough stochastic forcing to dominate fluctuations generated by other modes—spectral softness does not guarantee stochastic visibility. This is demonstrated in three ecological scenarios: a synthetic feasible community, an immigration-assembled community, and a diversification-generated community, all of which reach marginal stability without developing near-perfect pairwise correlations.
AI.motivation: Ecological communities are constantly reshaped by invasion, exclusion, and diversification, pushing them toward dynamical stability boundaries. Near such criticality, a soft mode is expected to dominate fluctuations and create strong abundance correlations, which have been proposed as early-warning signatures. The authors aim to test whether this expectation holds universally, as relying on such signatures could be misleading for ecological monitoring.
AI.method: The authors investigate whether spectral softness near marginal stability guarantees stochastic visibility of the soft mode in fluctuation patterns. They examine whether the soft mode receives enough environmental forcing to dominate the fluctuation background from all remaining modes, using three distinct ecological scenarios: a synthetic feasible community, a local community assembled via immigration from a regional pool, and a community generated through repeated diversification.
AI.result: In all three ecological scenarios, communities approach marginal stability without developing the near-perfect pairwise correlations predicted by the single-mode picture. This demonstrates that proximity to ecological criticality need not be visible in equal-time pairwise correlations, contradicting the previously proposed signature of imminent transitions.
AI.conclusion: The expectation that criticality produces dominant soft-mode fluctuations and strong pairwise correlations can fail even arbitrarily close to the stability boundary. Spectral softness is insufficient for stochastic visibility—the soft mode must also receive sufficient environmental forcing. Therefore, equal-time pairwise correlations are not a reliable indicator of proximity to ecological criticality.

title: PEtab SciML: an exchange format for specifying and training dynamic scientific machine learning models
summary: Summary: Dynamic scientific machine learning (SciML) models that combine mechanistic ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with machine learning (ML) components have applications ranging from learning unknown biological processes to integrating auxiliary data modalities into dynamic modelling. To enable reproducible and efficient SciML training, we introduce PEtab SciML, an interoperable data format for specifying parameter estimation problems in which mechanistic and ML model parameters are jointly estimated from time series data. PEtab SciML supports several ML ODE hybridization patterns in realistic problem setups. It is accompanied by a reference Python library and downstream modelling support in Python/JAX and Julia, provided by AMICI and PEtab.jl, respectively, and a collection of real data benchmarks. Availability and implementation: PEtab SciML is available on GitHub (https://github.com/PEtab-dev/petab_sciml). The reference Python package is installable from PyPI and is continuously tested and supported on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

AI.tldr: PEtab SciML is an interoperable data format for specifying parameter estimation problems in dynamic scientific machine learning (SciML), where mechanistic ODE models and ML components are jointly trained from time series data. It includes a reference Python library, downstream support in Python/JAX (AMICI) and Julia (PEtab.jl), and real-data benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Dynamic SciML models combining mechanistic ODEs with ML components are increasingly important, but there is a lack of standardized, reproducible, and efficient formats for specifying parameter estimation problems in this hybrid setting.
AI.method: The paper introduces PEtab SciML, a data format specification for parameter estimation problems, supporting multiple ML-ODE hybridization patterns. It provides a reference Python implementation and downstream tooling integration (AMICI in Python/JAX and PEtab.jl in Julia), along with a benchmark collection using realistic data.
AI.result: PEtab SciML is released on GitHub with an installable PyPI package, continuously tested across Linux, macOS, and Windows, providing a reproducible ecosystem for SciML parameter estimation.
AI.conclusion: PEtab SciML establishes a standardized interoperable format and tooling ecosystem to enable reproducible and efficient training of hybrid mechanistic-ML dynamic models.

title: Novel models of trait evolution via an expansion of Lande's fitness function: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process meets the Little Prince's boa
comment: Submitted to the Journal of the Society of Modeling and Theory in Population Biology
summary: Adaptive topographies form the foundation for much of our understanding of evolutionary change. Lande's 1976 influential paper on the adaptive topography of phenotypes demonstrated how the concept is inherent in both phenotypic and genetic models of evolution, and how the concept can be used to test evolutionary hypotheses given data. Here, we revisit and generalize Lande's original derivation of an equation analogous to Wright's genotypic adaptive topography to the case of two fitness components. A move to two fitness components yields novel predictions about the shape and mechanistic underpinnings of the adaptive topography. The optimum of this updated fitness function is a weighted average of the optima of the two fitness components, with weights given by the relative strengths of stabilizing selection on each component. Temporal or spatial heterogeneity in the strengths of selection for each fitness component create novel shapes (asymmetry, bi-modality, or lack thereof) of the overall fitness function, a possibility demonstrated with a case-study from the published literature. Finally, when combined with Lande's approach to generate an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model for the evolution of the average phenotype, our fitness formulation leads to a previously unrecognized family of stochastic differential equation models of trait evolution. These results provide mechanistic justification for non-Gaussian fitness functions (often observed in natural systems), provide a path for testing alternative models generating non-Gaussian fitness functions, and pave the way for future study of the interplay of ecological and evolutionary dynamics, such as in the study of evolutionary rescue.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits and generalizes Lande's 1976 adaptive topography framework from a single fitness component to two fitness components. The generalized model reveals that the overall fitness optimum is a weighted average of component optima, can produce novel fitness landscape shapes (asymmetry, bi-modality) under heterogeneous selection strengths, and leads to a new family of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck stochastic differential equation models for trait evolution.
AI.motivation: Lande's 1976 adaptive topography concept is foundational to evolutionary biology, but the original derivation assumes a single fitness component. The authors aim to generalize this framework to two fitness components to generate novel predictions about fitness landscape shape, mechanistic underpinnings, and trait evolution models that better reflect natural systems.
AI.method: The authors mathematically revisit Lande's derivation and extend it to the case of two fitness components. The overall fitness optimum is derived as a weighted average of component optima, weighted by the relative strengths of stabilizing selection. The framework is then combined with Lande's approach to generate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck models, and the resulting fitness function shapes are demonstrated with a published case study.
AI.result: Two fitness components yield: (1) a fitness optimum that is a weighted average of the two component optima; (2) novel fitness function shapes including asymmetry and bi-modality when selection strengths vary temporally or spatially; (3) a previously unrecognized family of stochastic differential equation (OU) models of trait evolution.
AI.conclusion: The generalized framework provides mechanistic justification for non-Gaussian fitness functions observed in nature, offers a path for testing alternative models that generate such non-Gaussian fitness, and opens avenues for studying ecological-evolutionary dynamics including evolutionary rescue.

title: Automatic bioinformatic software named entity recognition from literature
summary: Bioinformatics software and databases are essential components of modern life science research, yet their mentions in the scientific literature are often inconsistent and difficult to systematically identify at scale. The lack of a comprehensive and up-to-date catalog of bioinformatics resources hinders efforts toward automated biomedical knowledge extraction and streamlined data analysis. Here we present SNAIL, a hybrid named entity recognition framework designed to automatically identify bioinformatics software and database (SW/DB) names from biomedical texts. SNAIL integrates complementary lexical and semantic modeling strategies. The lexical component captures orthographic patterns and contextual cues characteristic of SW/DB names, while the semantic component leverages contextual embeddings generated by transformer-based language models such as SciBERT, combined with an explicit token-masking strategy to enhance entity-focused representations. A large training corpus was constructed automatically through a hybrid pipeline that integrates citation-hinted extraction with large language model-assisted distillation. Evaluation on two independent benchmark datasets and real-world research articles demonstrates that SNAIL substantially outperforms existing approaches, including domain-specific methods such as bioNerDS2 and general-purpose large language models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude. Applying SNAIL to large-scale literature analysis further reveals distinct journal-level preferences across bioinformatics subfields. These results demonstrate that SNAIL provides an accurate and scalable solution for identifying bioinformatics resources in scientific texts and enables systematic meta-analysis of tool usage and research trends.

AI.tldr: SNAIL is a hybrid named entity recognition framework that combines lexical and semantic modeling strategies (including transformer-based embeddings and token masking) to automatically identify bioinformatics software and database names in biomedical texts, substantially outperforming existing approaches including bioNerDS2 and general-purpose LLMs.
AI.motivation: Bioinformatics software and database mentions in scientific literature are inconsistent and difficult to identify systematically at scale, and the lack of a comprehensive, up-to-date catalog hinders automated biomedical knowledge extraction and streamlined data analysis.
AI.method: SNAIL integrates a lexical component capturing orthographic patterns and contextual cues with a semantic component using transformer-based contextual embeddings (e.g., SciBERT) combined with an explicit token-masking strategy. Training data is constructed automatically via a hybrid pipeline combining citation-hinted extraction with LLM-assisted distillation.
AI.result: SNAIL substantially outperforms existing approaches (including bioNerDS2 and general-purpose LLMs such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, and Claude) on two independent benchmark datasets and real-world research articles, and reveals distinct journal-level preferences across bioinformatics subfields in large-scale analysis.
AI.conclusion: SNAIL provides an accurate and scalable solution for identifying bioinformatics resources in scientific texts and enables systematic meta-analysis of tool usage and research trends.

title: Quantum Kernel Estimation for the Discovery of Early Lung Cancer Detection
summary:
Lung cancer screening with low-dose chest computed tomography reduces mortality, but its impact is limited by uptake, adherence, and management challenges. Blood-based cell-free DNA (cfDNA) biomarkers offer a complementary approach, although early detection remains difficult because of lung cancer heterogeneity and high-dimensional, nonlinear molecular signals. We evaluated quantum-classical hybrid machine learning for lung cancer detection using DNA fragmentomics and DNA methylation. After feature selection, models were trained using 20- and 40-feature subsets. Features were encoded into quantum Hilbert space using angle and dense-angle feature maps with multiple entanglement strategies. Fidelity-based quantum kernels were computed with exact statevector simulation and integrated with precomputed-kernel SVM and kernel-PCA logistic regression and compared with an SVM model trained on the original features.
  This framework enabled systematic evaluation of how encoding and entanglement design affect classification. Across repeated held-out evaluations, quantum-kernel models achieved competitive performance on both datasets. For fragmentomics, several 20-feature configurations improved AUC relative to a classical SVM baseline, suggesting effective capture of nonlinear cfDNA fragmentation structure. For methylation, the classical SVM achieved the highest AUC, although selected quantum models remained competitive and improved specificity in some cases. Increasing features from 20 to 40 did not consistently improve performance and often increased variability. Overall, these results support quantum kernel methods as a promising approach for cfDNA-based lung cancer detection.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates quantum-classical hybrid machine learning for lung cancer detection using cfDNA fragmentomics and methylation data, demonstrating that quantum-kernel models achieve competitive performance compared to classical SVM baselines.
AI.motivation: Lung cancer screening reduces mortality but is limited by uptake, adherence, and management challenges. Blood-based cfDNA biomarkers offer a complementary approach, yet early detection remains difficult due to lung cancer heterogeneity and high-dimensional, nonlinear molecular signals.
AI.method: The authors evaluate quantum-classical hybrid machine learning using DNA fragmentomics and DNA methylation. After feature selection (20- and 40-feature subsets), features are encoded into quantum Hilbert space using angle and dense-angle feature maps with multiple entanglement strategies. Fidelity-based quantum kernels are computed via exact statevector simulation and integrated with precomputed-kernel SVM and kernel-PCA logistic regression, compared against a classical SVM baseline.
AI.result: Quantum-kernel models achieved competitive performance on both datasets. For fragmentomics, several 20-feature configurations improved AUC relative to classical SVM. For methylation, classical SVM achieved the highest AUC, though selected quantum models remained competitive and improved specificity in some cases. Increasing features from 20 to 40 did not consistently improve performance and often increased variability.
AI.conclusion: Quantum kernel methods are a promising approach for cfDNA-based lung cancer detection, capable of capturing nonlinear molecular structures effectively, with encoding and entanglement design significantly affecting classification outcomes.

title: Longitudinal Bayesian Learning of Continuous Disease Position across the Alzheimer's Disease Continuum
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progresses as a continuous biological process, whereas most existing neuroimaging-based artificial intelligence methods remain limited to discrete diagnosis or clinical score prediction from cross-sectional imaging. In this work, we propose Disease Continuum Positioning (DCP), a longitudinal Bayesian Learning framework that continuously estimates disease severity from longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). Specifically, DCP models disease severity as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable by jointly integrating longitudinal observations with weak clinical supervision, from which the proposed Disease Continuum Score (DCS) is derived to quantify an individual's position along the Alzheimer's disease continuum together with its associated uncertainty. Extensive experiments on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort demonstrate that DCP consistently outperforms representative disease progression methods. More importantly, comprehensive validation analyses show that DCS accurately characterizes disease severity, exhibits strong clinical relevance, preserves longitudinal disease evolution, and predicts future disease conversion. These results suggest that DCS provides a quantitative imaging-derived representation for continuous assessment of Alzheimer's disease progression beyond conventional diagnostic labels and clinical scores.

AI.tldr: Proposes Disease Continuum Positioning (DCP), a longitudinal Bayesian learning framework that estimates continuous Alzheimer's disease severity from longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) using low-dimensional probabilistic latent variables with weak clinical supervision, yielding a Disease Continuum Score (DCS) with uncertainty quantification that outperforms existing methods on ADNI data.
AI.motivation: AD progresses as a continuous biological process, yet existing neuroimaging AI methods are limited to discrete diagnosis or cross-sectional clinical score prediction, failing to capture the continuous nature of disease progression over time.
AI.method: DCP models disease severity as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable by jointly integrating longitudinal DTI observations with weak clinical supervision. A Disease Continuum Score (DCS) is derived to quantify an individual's position along the AD continuum with associated uncertainty.
AI.result: On the ADNI cohort, DCP consistently outperforms representative disease progression methods. DCS accurately characterizes disease severity, shows strong clinical relevance, preserves longitudinal disease evolution, and predicts future disease conversion.
AI.conclusion: DCS provides a quantitative imaging-derived representation for continuous assessment of AD progression beyond conventional diagnostic labels and clinical scores.

title: Resource-Efficient Bio-Molecular Docking on a NISQ-era Digital Quantum Computer
summary: Molecular docking is a vital computational task in drug discovery, wherein the objective is to efficiently identify optimal binding poses between a ligand and a target receptor protein. Due to the combinatorial explosion of possible binding configurations, docking of large and flexible molecules remains a computationally intensive problem, especially at scale. Early studies have revealed that the molecular docking can be re-cast as a maximum vertex-weighted clique problem (MVWCP) problem on a compatibility graph to be solved classically. In this work, we proposed a hybrid quantum-classical approach for molecular docking leveraging the MVWCP formalism with a variational full-basis encoding (FBE) strategy, which enables efficient encoding of classical binary variables with Bloch sphere vectors. We further prove that a global minimizer of the FBE objective can always be chosen to be a pure product state, thereby providing a rigorous justification for its optimization using a unitary variational circuit. The molecular docking problem is first mapped to a cost Hamiltonian that is minimized within a variational framework, optimized via a randomized imaginary time evolution (ITE)-inspired warm start, and gradient-based techniques. Finally, we also executed the circuit on an IBM quantum computer, underlying the feasibility and of quantum-assisted optimization for structure-based drug design and point towards the broader utility of advanced encoding techniques in quantum optimization for computational biology.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical approach for molecular docking, reformulated as a maximum vertex-weighted clique problem (MVWCP), using a variational full-basis encoding (FBE) strategy with randomized imaginary time evolution warm starts, and demonstrates feasibility on IBM quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Molecular docking is computationally intensive, especially for large flexible molecules, due to combinatorial explosion of binding configurations. The authors aim to leverage quantum computing to address this scalability challenge by re-casting docking as an optimization problem suitable for quantum solvers.
AI.method: 1. Re-cast molecular docking as a maximum vertex-weighted clique problem (MVWCP) on a compatibility graph. 2. Map the problem to a cost Hamiltonian and optimize it within a variational framework using full-basis encoding (FBE), which encodes classical binary variables with Bloch sphere vectors. 3. Prove that a global minimizer of the FBE objective can always be a pure product state, justifying unitary variational circuit optimization. 4. Apply randomized imaginary time evolution (ITE)-inspired warm starts and gradient-based techniques. 5. Execute the final circuit on an IBM quantum computer.
AI.result: The variational FBE approach successfully solves the molecular docking problem, with rigorous proof that global minimizers exist as pure product states. The ITE-inspired warm start and gradient-based optimization yield valid results, and execution on an IBM quantum computer demonstrates practical feasibility of quantum-assisted docking.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid quantum-classical framework with FBE is a feasible and promising approach for molecular docking, showcasing the broader utility of advanced encoding techniques in quantum optimization for computational biology and structure-based drug design.

title: Bringing analytic rigor to agentic AI for science: The Brain Researcher platform for neuroimaging data analysis
summary: AI agents can execute scientific analyses, but an analytic output becomes a defensible claim only after alternatives are weighed and the claim is limited to what the evidence supports. Agents may reproduce failures including selective analysis, premature declarations of success and optimization of imperfect criteria. We present Brain Researcher, an agentic research harness operating in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under rules for admissible analyses, required checks and claim scope. In benchmarks, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy across seven models by 70.2 percentage points (23.3% without it versus 93.6% with it) and verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In collaborator-led and self-evolving studies, multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review classified claims as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected or deferred. By linking decisions to evidence and provenance, Brain Researcher embeds methodological judgment within the workflow, not after it.

AI.tldr: Brain Researcher is an agentic research harness for neuroimaging that enforces rules for admissible analyses, required checks, and claim scope, improving tool-selection accuracy from 23.3% to 93.6% across seven models and increasing verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. It embeds methodological judgment directly into the workflow via multiverse analyses and provenance-linked claim review.
AI.motivation: AI agents can execute scientific analyses, but often produce outputs that are not defensible claims because they may engage in selective analysis, premature declarations of success, and optimization of imperfect criteria. There is a need to constrain agent behavior so that analytic outputs become properly weighed and scoped scientific claims.
AI.method: Brain Researcher is an agentic research harness that operates in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under explicit rules for admissible analyses, required checks, and claim scope. It incorporates multiverse analyses to expose analytic-choice sensitivity and uses scientific review to classify claims into six categories (accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected, deferred), while linking decisions to evidence and provenance.
AI.result: Across seven models, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy by 70.2 percentage points (from 23.3% without it to 93.6% with it) and improved verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In collaborator-led and self-evolving studies, multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review classified claims into six categories.
AI.conclusion: By linking decisions to evidence and provenance, Brain Researcher embeds methodological judgment within the workflow rather than after it, enabling agents to produce claims that are properly scoped and defensible given the evidence.

title: Flow Matching Meets 3D Curvilinear Structure Segmentation in Medical Imaging
comment: International Workshop on Machine Learning in Medical Imaging (MLMI 2026) @ MICCAI
summary: Segmentation of curvilinear anatomical structures in 3D medical images remains challenging due to complex topology, severe class imbalance, weak contrast, and large variations in structure morphology. While deep learning approaches for 3D curvilinear segmentation have been proposed, they are often tailored to specific anatomies or modalities, limiting generalization across clinical settings and leaving room for improvement. Recent generative models have shown the benefits of iterative prediction for structured segmentation tasks, yet diffusion-based methods suffer from computationally expensive sampling, hindering their use on high-resolution 3D volumes. We present 3D-CurvSegFlow, a flow matching-based model for 3D curvilinear structure segmentation. The model learns a continuous transformation from a simple source distribution to the target vascular representation, enabling progressive refinement of complex curvilinear geometries with efficient inference. We evaluate our method on Three public challenging datasets covering distinct anatomies and modalities: portal vein, cerebral vessel, and coronary arteries. Using a common architecture and training strategy across all tasks, our method outperforms general-purpose and vessel-specific approaches, with strong preservation of thin branches and vascular continuity. This work not only advances the state-of-the-art in 3D curvilinear segmentation but also opens new avenues for efficient, generalizable, and clinically applicable methods in medical image analysis.

AI.tldr: 3D-CurvSegFlow is a flow matching-based deep learning model for 3D curvilinear structure segmentation (e.g., vessels) in medical images, which learns a continuous transformation from a simple distribution to the target vascular representation for progressive refinement with efficient inference. It outperforms general-purpose and vessel-specific methods across three public datasets covering different anatomies (portal vein, cerebral vessel, coronary arteries) using a unified architecture.
AI.motivation: 3D curvilinear anatomical structure segmentation is challenging due to complex topology, severe class imbalance, weak contrast, and morphological variation. Existing deep learning methods are often anatomy- or modality-specific, and diffusion-based generative approaches suffer from computationally expensive sampling that hinders use on high-resolution 3D volumes.
AI.method: The model is based on flow matching, learning a continuous transformation from a simple source distribution to the target vascular representation. This enables progressive refinement of complex curvilinear geometries while maintaining efficient inference, unlike diffusion-based methods.
AI.result: Evaluated on three public datasets (portal vein, cerebral vessel, coronary arteries), the method outperforms both general-purpose and vessel-specific approaches, demonstrating strong preservation of thin branches and vascular continuity with a unified architecture and training strategy across all tasks.
AI.conclusion: The work advances state-of-the-art 3D curvilinear segmentation and provides efficient, generalizable, and clinically applicable methods for medical image analysis.

title: Emergence of cooperation: A reputation-modulated reinforcement learning
summary: Reputation is widely recognized as a key mechanism for sustaining cooperation. However, most existing game-theoretic models treat reputation primarily as an external factor that modulates payoffs, interaction structures, or strategy update rules. In many social contexts, though, reputation operates primarily as information -- it shapes how individuals interpret their own experiences and assess the behavior of others. To bridge this gap, we propose a spatial prisoner's dilemma game grounded in the reinforcement learning paradigm, in which agents equipped with Q-learning integrate both individual and social information via a locally defined reputation metric to guide their decisions. Our results reveal that reputation-modulated learning significantly promotes the emergence of cooperative behavior, and we observe a discontinuous phase transition from full cooperation to full defection as the temptation increases. Cooperation spreads through the nucleation of cooperative clusters, whereas the disintegration of these clusters drives the system into an absorbing state of complete defection. Overall, this study demonstrates that reputation facilitates cooperation not only by providing direct incentives but also by reshaping the social information landscape that agents rely on for learning and adaptation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a spatial prisoner's dilemma game with Q-learning agents that integrate individual and social information via a local reputation metric. Results show reputation-modulated learning promotes cooperation with a discontinuous phase transition from full cooperation to full defection, driven by cooperative cluster nucleation and disintegration.
AI.motivation: Existing game-theoretic models treat reputation primarily as an external factor modifying payoffs, interaction structures, or update rules, but in many social contexts reputation operates as information—shaping how individuals interpret experiences and assess others. This gap motivates a new framework where reputation influences learning and adaptation.
AI.method: A spatial prisoner's dilemma game is built on a reinforcement learning paradigm, where agents equipped with Q-learning combine individual and social information through a locally defined reputation metric to guide decision-making.
AI.result: Reputation-modulated learning significantly promotes cooperative behavior. A discontinuous phase transition from full cooperation to full defection is observed as temptation increases. Cooperation spreads via nucleation of cooperative clusters, while cluster disintegration leads to an absorbing state of complete defection.
AI.conclusion: Reputation facilitates cooperation not only through direct incentives but also by reshaping the social information landscape that agents rely on for learning and adaptation.

title: Climate change and human mobility will shape dengue emergence risk in Europe
summary: The risk of local arbovirus outbreaks in Europe is expected to increase due to climate change, as suggested by the multiplication of arbovirus outbreaks in the last decades. Europe has historically been a non-endemic region, making it vital to pinpoint which populations are potentially exposed -and under which conditions- so we can build truly robust epidemic preparedness capabilities. We introduce an integrated, multi-scale model that fuses a mechanistic transmission engine with a vector abundance framework, all embedded in a mobility-driven metapopulation system capturing human, vector, and air-traffic movement. To this end, we combine climate and population projections with mobility data to estimate and map dengue emergence risk in Europe throughout the 21st century. Additionally, we introduce a dedicated migration model that explores how climate-driven population redistribution could alter these risk estimates.Assuming the climate avoids major tipping points, model-derived risk indicators increase substantially under most emissions scenarios. While the spatio-temporal risk will remain largely driven by importation, our results indicate a gradual transition toward an environment-driven regime, particularly under the worst-case emissions scenario. To better anticipate and manage recurrent arbovirus outbreaks, our findings highlight the need to integrate mobility pathways and climate-driven population redistribution into predictive models of vector-borne disease emergence in temperate regions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an integrated multi-scale model combining mechanistic transmission, vector abundance, and mobility-driven metapopulation dynamics to estimate dengue emergence risk in Europe throughout the 21st century under climate change, showing substantial risk increases that transition from importation-driven to environment-driven regimes.
AI.motivation: Europe is historically non-endemic for arboviruses, but climate change is increasing outbreak risk. Robust epidemic preparedness requires identifying which populations are potentially exposed and under what conditions.
AI.method: The authors develop an integrated multi-scale model fusing a mechanistic transmission engine with a vector abundance framework, embedded in a mobility-driven metapopulation system that captures human, vector, and air-traffic movement. They combine climate and population projections with mobility data, and introduce a migration model to explore how climate-driven population redistribution could alter risk estimates.
AI.result: Assuming climate avoids major tipping points, model-derived risk indicators increase substantially under most emissions scenarios. Risk remains largely importation-driven but shows a gradual transition toward an environment-driven regime, particularly under worst-case emissions.
AI.conclusion: Predictive models of vector-borne disease emergence in temperate regions must integrate mobility pathways and climate-driven population redistribution to better anticipate and manage recurrent arbovirus outbreaks.

title: Growth phases of an active tissue: determinate, indeterminate, and proportionate
summary: Growth may cease at a target size or continue throughout life: the determinate and indeterminate phenotypes. We develop an active viscoelastic continuum model of a tissue growing along one axis, in which cell division and death generate active stresses. We find two asymptotic states: one in which the tissue reaches a relative size fixed by its material parameters, and one in which it elongates linearly without bound. Which state is realised is set by the ratio of active stress to elastic modulus. The transition originates in a bound on the elastic stress the tissue can support: a sufficiently large activity can never be balanced. In a tissue made of parts with different material properties, the growing phase settles into fixed length proportions, set by the mechanical impedances of the parts rather than inherited; matching impedances to initial lengths preserves the proportions the tissue began with. Determinate, indeterminate and proportionate growth thus appear as regimes of one continuum mechanical framework.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an active viscoelastic continuum model of tissue growth along one axis, showing that determinate (finite) and indeterminate (unbounded linear) growth emerge as two asymptotic regimes determined by the ratio of active stress to elastic modulus, and that proportionality in composite tissues is set by mechanical impedance rather than inherited properties.
AI.motivation: To understand why some tissues stop growing at a target size (determinate growth) while others grow continuously (indeterminate growth), and how growth proportions are established in heterogeneous tissues, within a unified mechanical framework rather than separate biological mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors develop an active viscoelastic continuum model of a tissue growing along one axis, where cell division and death generate active stresses. They analyze the asymptotic behavior of the model and examine tissues composed of parts with different material properties.
AI.result: Two asymptotic states are found: one where the tissue reaches a finite relative size determined by material parameters, and one where it elongates linearly without bound. The transition is determined by the ratio of active stress to elastic modulus, arising from a bound on elastic stress the tissue can support. In composite tissues, growing phases settle into fixed length proportions set by mechanical impedances, not inheritance; matching impedances to initial lengths preserves initial proportions.
AI.conclusion: Determinate, indeterminate, and proportionate growth all emerge as regimes of a single continuum mechanical framework, unifying these seemingly distinct growth phenomena under one mathematical description.

title: Decoding silent reading from non-invasive EEG
comment: 45 pages (including 12 pages of Supplementary Material), 11 figures (including 2 in Supplementary Material)
summary: Non-invasive decoding of inner speech faces a fundamental data problem: a corpus pairing brain activity with a person's spontaneous inner monologue cannot be collected, and the available proxy paradigms (cued repetitive and retrospectively reported generative inner speech) are slow to acquire, poorly time-locked, and subject compliance is unverifiable. We therefore treat silent reading as a scalable proxy task and ask how much lexical and semantic information a contrastive decoder can extract from it. We report an open-vocabulary analysis of approximately 240,000 word presentations recorded from a single densely-sampled participant across 393 runs (ca. 49 h) of 19-channel dry-electrode EEG. Words from continuous narrative text were presented in rapid serial visual presentation, with typography randomised on every trial to partially decorrelate word identity from low-level visual form. A convolutional EEG encoder, optionally followed by a causal transformer, was trained with a CLIP-style contrastive objective to align short EEG windows with hidden-state embeddings of the presented word taken from a large language model. Decoding, evaluated as word-grouped top-10 retrieval against permutation baselines, was reliably above chance, extended to mid-frequency and rare words, and scaled log-linearly with training-data volume with no sign of saturation. Removing occipital and posterior-temporal electrodes reduced the word-level gain by roughly one third but left context tracking unchanged. Control analyses separate word-level decoding from narrative context tracking and from a non-neural positional prior introduced by the transformer's positional embedding. These results establish that open-vocabulary word-level information is recoverable from EEG during silent reading, and that decoding is data-limited rather than saturated.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates open-vocabulary word-level decoding from EEG during silent reading using a contrastive learning approach, showing that lexical and semantic information is recoverable at scale (~240k word presentations from a single participant) and that decoding performance scales log-linearly with data volume without saturation.
AI.motivation: Decoding inner speech from brain activity is fundamentally limited by the inability to collect ground-truth corpora of spontaneous inner monologue paired with brain signals. Existing proxy paradigms (cued repetitive and retrospectively reported generative inner speech) are slow, poorly time-locked, and have unverifiable compliance. The authors therefore identify silent reading as a scalable proxy task to study how much lexical and semantic information can be extracted from brain signals.
AI.method: A single participant read continuous narrative text in rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) while ~240,000 word presentations were recorded from 19-channel dry-electrode EEG across 393 runs (~49 h). Typography was randomized per trial to decorrelate word identity from low-level visual form. A convolutional EEG encoder (optionally followed by a causal transformer) was trained with a CLIP-style contrastive objective to align short EEG windows with LLM hidden-state embeddings of the presented word. Decoding was evaluated as word-grouped top-10 retrieval against permutation baselines.
AI.result: Decoding was reliably above chance, extended to mid-frequency and rare words, and scaled log-linearly with training data with no sign of saturation. Removing occipital and posterior-temporal electrodes reduced word-level gain by ~1/3 but did not affect context tracking. Control analyses separated word-level decoding from narrative context tracking and from a positional prior in the transformer.
AI.conclusion: Open-vocabulary word-level information is recoverable from EEG during silent reading, establishing silent reading as a viable scalable proxy for inner-speech decoding research. Current decoding performance is data-limited rather than saturated, suggesting further gains are possible with additional data.

title: GENIE: Generative Neural Inference for Epidemics
summary: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic highlighted the ongoing risk infectious diseases pose to society and the value of reliable information on the likely future burden. When forecasting an epidemic at fine spatial resolution, traditionally used mechanistic compartmental model struggle to capture highly complex granular transmission dynamics, resulting in inaccurate and overconfident forecasts. However, detailed Agent-Based Models (ABMs), are challenging to calibrate and are too computationally expensive to use in real-time. Amortized simulation-based inference promises to overcome this difficulty by exploiting the power of machine learning (ML) to perform approximate forecasting at near-real-time using arbitrarily complex models of epidemics. In this work we introduce Generative Neural Inference for Epidemics (GENIE), a spatio-temporal ML-based framework for high-resolution forecasting of the burden of respiratory pathogens. GENIE is designed to reflect two key characteristics of outbreaks: (i) shared biological mechanisms across locations and (ii) location-specific characteristics affecting transmission dynamics. This results in the model architecture having two modules: (i) a Local Infection Encoder - which learns to represent disease dynamics shared across all locations and (ii) a Local Profile Encoder - which learns location-specific representations. Using simulations from a high-resolution spatio-temporal ABM, GENIE is trained to generate samples from an approximate posterior predictive distribution of future epidemic trajectories. Benchmarked against established statistical and ML models, GENIE demonstrates superior performance across a range of measures including the timing and magnitude of peak hospitalisations.

AI.tldr: GENIE (Generative Neural Inference for Epidemics) is a spatio-temporal ML-based framework for high-resolution forecasting of respiratory pathogen burden, trained via amortized simulation-based inference on high-resolution ABM simulations to generate approximate posterior predictive samples of future epidemic trajectories.
AI.motivation: Traditional compartmental models struggle to capture highly complex granular transmission dynamics at fine spatial resolution, while detailed Agent-Based Models are too computationally expensive for real-time calibration and forecasting.
AI.method: GENIE uses a two-module architecture: (i) a Local Infection Encoder that learns shared biological disease dynamics across locations, and (ii) a Local Profile Encoder that learns location-specific representations. It is trained via amortized simulation-based inference on simulations from a high-resolution spatio-temporal ABM to generate samples from an approximate posterior predictive distribution.
AI.result: GENIE demonstrates superior performance against established statistical and ML benchmark models across various measures, including the timing and magnitude of peak hospitalisations.
AI.conclusion: Amortized simulation-based inference combined with a modular neural architecture can enable near-real-time, high-resolution epidemic forecasting using arbitrarily complex models, overcoming the computational bottlenecks of traditional ABM calibration.
